title: Container ship sinks in Strait of Hormuz as Iran steps up attacks
description: Vessels transit the Hormuz Strait off the coast of Iran's southern port city of Bandar Abbas on September 7, 2026.Atta Kenare | Afp | Getty ImagesA co
body: Vessels transit the Hormuz Strait off the coast of Iran's southern port city of Bandar Abbas on September 7, 2026.Atta Kenare | Afp | Getty ImagesA container ship sank in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday as Iran escalated its attacks on commercial vessels.The GFS Pride, registered in Singapore, sank after it was struck by an unidentified projectile and caught fire. The ship's 21 crew members were safely evacuated and no injuries were reported, according to the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore. "Such attacks are unprovoked, unjustifiable and a breach of international law," the Singapore maritime authority said in a statement Wednesday. Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed early Wednesday that a container ship exploded and sank after hitting a naval mine, according to the state news agency Tasnim. But there is no independent evidence to confirm that a mine is what caused the Pride to sink, according to the maritime security firm Marisks. Iran's claims are "consistent with an ongoing psychological operations campaign aimed at generating fear, increasing uncertainty and discouraging commercial shipping" in Hormuz, Marisks said in a security alert.Iran has escalated its strikes on commercial ships transiting Hormuz in recent weeks, as it tries to choke off a rebound in crude oil exports through the strait. More than 20 vessels, mostly oil tankers, have come under attack this month in Hormuz, the Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman, according to incident reports from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre. The attacks this month have left two sailors missing and 12 injured, according to the International Maritime Organization, a United Nations' agency. Crude oil exports through Hormuz hit prewar levels in September as the U.S. military guided tankers through the strait, but shipments have since pulled back as attacks have increased.  Crude exports through Hormuz averaged 8.5 million barrels per day (bpd) in the week ended Oct. 12, nearly 40% below normal levels before the Iran war, according to data from Kpler. Shipments from the entire region, including pipelines to the Gulf of Oman and Red Sea, stood at 14 million bpd, or nearly 20% below prewar levels, the data showed. Daily flows are volatile, with only 3 million barrels of crude transiting Hormuz on Monday while 6 million barrels passed through the strait on Friday, according to Kpler.

schema.headline: Container ship sinks in Strait of Hormuz as Iran steps up attacks

title: Fannie Mae sharply raises mortgage rate forecast for 2027
description: Aerial view of single family homes line the streets on April 2, 2026 in Thousand Oaks, California.Kevin Carter | Getty ImagesEconomists at Fannie Mae
body: Aerial view of single family homes line the streets on April 2, 2026 in Thousand Oaks, California.Kevin Carter | Getty ImagesEconomists at Fannie Mae are now predicting much higher mortgage rates through the end of 2026 and into 2027. It now puts the average rate on the 30-year fixed at 7.4% for the fourth quarter of this year and 7.5% through all of next year. It previously forecast 6.8% for the fourth quarter and 6.7% for all of next year. The average rate on the 30-year fixed stood at 7.46% Tuesday, according to Mortgage News Daily, but will likely move higher today. Bond yields are rising after a hotter-than-expected inflation report. Mortgage rates have been rising sharply since the start of September, as inflation remains stubbornly high and bond markets sell off due to several factors. The Federal Reserve also raised its benchmark rate for the first time in more than three years. Mortgage rates do not follow the Fed's rate exactly, but they do react to how the central bank sees inflation going forward. Mortgage rates loosely follow the yield on the 10-year Treasury, which has been rising sharply on higher oil prices and growing concerns in the global economy. Get Property Play directly to your inboxCNBC's Property Play with Diana Olick covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, delivered weekly to your inbox.Subscribe here to get access today.Higher rates have already put the housing market in an early deep freeze this fall. Pending sales, counted by signed contracts on existing homes, were down 8.5% in September year-over-year, according to Zillow. Mortgage demand continues to drop sharply, as buyers face higher prices and weakening affordability. Not only can fewer buyers now afford a home, but fewer can qualify for a mortgage. Fannie Mae did not respond to requests for comment on its latest forecast.

schema.headline: Fannie Mae sharply raises mortgage rate forecast for 2027

title: Even more borrowers choose riskier mortgages, as higher interest rates crush affordability
description: In an aerial view, two-story single family homes line the streets of neighborhood on Jan. 13, 2026 in Thousand Oaks, California.Kevin Carter | Getty I
body: In an aerial view, two-story single family homes line the streets of neighborhood on Jan. 13, 2026 in Thousand Oaks, California.Kevin Carter | Getty ImagesMortgage rates moved to the highest level in nearly three years last week, causing overall demand to drop. Riskier mortgages, however, continue to gain a growing share of what demand there is.Total mortgage application volume dropped 2.7% last week compared with the previous week, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association's seasonally adjusted index. It is also 37.5% lower than the same week one year ago. The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loan balances, $832,750 or less, increased to 7.50% from 7.49%, with points decreasing to 0.83 from 0.84, including the origination fee, for loans with a 20% down payment. The rate was more than a full percentage point higher than it was a year ago. "As a result, borrowers continue to rely more on ARM [adjustable-rate mortgage] loans to help lower their monthly payments," said Joel Kan, an MBA economist, in a release. "The ARM share at 10.5 percent was at its highest level since October 2025." ARMs offer lower interest rates and can be fixed for up to 10 years, but then they adjust depending on future interest rates. That is why they are considered riskier.Applications to refinance a home loan have been hit hardest by higher rates, as a shrinking pool of borrowers can now find much relief. These applications declined 0.4% for the week and were 56% lower year over year.Get Property Play directly to your inboxCNBC's Property Play with Diana Olick covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, delivered weekly to your inbox.Subscribe here to get access today.Applications for a mortgage to purchase a home fell 4% for the week and were 16% lower than the same week one year ago. There are more homes available for sale now, but mostly on the higher end of the market. Supply is also rising not because of new listings, but because of slower sales. Home prices also continue to rise.While closed home sales increased very slightly in September from August, according to a report Tuesday from the National Association of Realtors, those sales were based on market conditions over the summer, when rates were lower. "Despite the small monthly gain on a seasonally adjusted basis, August and September marked the two slowest months for home sales this year," said Lawrence Yun, NAR's chief economist, in a release. "Further increases in mortgage rates in recent weeks mean fewer buyers can qualify to purchase a home."Correction: Total mortgage application volume dropped 2.7% last week compared with the previous week. An earlier version misstated the figure. Closed home sales increased very slightly in September from August. An earlier version misstated the timeline.

title: Iran says it’s ‘counting the moments’ until it can strike U.S. warships; Saudi Aramco facilities attacked
description: The USS Abraham Lincoln, pictured on Oct. 8 in San Diego, set a U.S. Navy record spending over 260 days consecutively at sea without a port call while
body: The USS Abraham Lincoln, pictured on Oct. 8 in San Diego, set a U.S. Navy record spending over 260 days consecutively at sea without a port call while playing a key role in Operation Epic Fury and regional maritime security operations in the Middle East. Justin Sullivan | Getty ImagesSaudi officials said Wednesday that an administrative building belonging to oil giant Saudi Aramco was targeted overnight, as the Tehran-backed Houthi militants step up their attacks on the kingdom. The strike caused a fire, but no injuries were reported at the site in the city of Dhahran on the country's eastern coast, according to a statement from the Saudi Arabian Ministry of Energy. The Houthis, a Yemen-based militia group backed by Iran, have launched a series of strikes on Saudi Arabian targets over the past week. Airport attacks in the capital city of Riyadh led to multiple fatalities, flight cancellations and property damage. Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport remains closed until Saturday.Yemen's civil war has returned to full-scale fighting between the Houthis and the country's internationally recognized government amid a wider regional escalation linked to the U.S.–Iran war.Iran 'counting the moments' until it can attack U.S. shipsIslamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) chief Ali Ozmaei said Wednesday that Tehran is "counting the moments" until it can sink American warships, according to Iranian state-affiliated media. "If the Americans think the Strait of Hormuz is open, let them come closer. We are impatient to sink American warships," Ozmaei reportedly said in a televised interview. "We are waiting for U.S. warships to approach the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz so we can sink them. We are counting down every moment until this happens."CNBC has reached out to the White House for comment. The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that the Islamic Republic has been strengthening defenses around sensitive locations like nuclear sites, and telling regional officials that Tehran will respond to any new U.S. strikes with retaliatory measures across the Middle East as it prepares its population for renewed war in the coming weeks. U.S. President Donald Trump said Tuesday that American forces would not attack Iran before the midterm election, which will take place on Nov. 3.On Wednesday, reports emerged that a cargo ship caught fire and sank in the Strait of Hormuz after hitting a naval mine as it attempted to transit the waterway. CNBC was not able to independently verify the reports.  Later on Wednesday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations — a Royal Navy-sponsored maritime security organization — said a "verified source" reported that a container ship had been struck by an "unknown projectile."In a post on X overnight, U.S. Central Command refuted Iranian claims that the strait is under Iran's control. "IRGC's navy commander has no navy. American forces and regional partners clearly control the Strait of Hormuz," Centcom said. "Just yesterday U.S. forces assisted Gulf partners in shipping more than 19 million barrels of crude oil through the strait."

schema.headline: Iran says it’s ‘counting the moments’ until it can strike U.S. warships; Saudi Aramco facilities attacked

title: Bending Spoons skyrockets 35% as Berkshire Hathaway makes $330 million investment
description: Matteo Danieli, co-founder of Bending Spoons, center, during the company's initial public offering (IPO) at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York, US, on
body: Matteo Danieli, co-founder of Bending Spoons, center, during the company's initial public offering (IPO) at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York, US, on Wednesday, July 1, 2026. Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesShares of Bending Spoons skyrocketed 35% after a new securities filing revealed that Berkshire Hathaway made a fresh $330 million investment into the company.The latest infusion follows the conglomerate's $600 million investment from July, when the Italy-based serial acquirer went public on the Nasdaq.Under the deal, Bending Spoons will issue 10 million ordinary shares to Berkshire at $33 a share. "Bending Spoons continuously evaluates M&A opportunities, and our pipeline remains strong," said Francesco Patarnello, Bending Spoons' co-founder and head of business acquisitions, in a statement. "We believe Berkshire Hathaway's investment reflects confidence in our team and Platform and will further enhance our financial flexibility and ability to pursue attractive acquisitions as part of our broader financing strategy."The investment now brings Berkshire's stake in the company to 4%, according to the filing, and is the conglomerate's latest investment decision as CEO Greg Abel took the helm from founder and legendary investor Warren Buffett at the start of the year. title: JPMorgan Chase blocks outside AI agents like Muse, Instinct from directly accessing accounts
description: Jamie Dimon, CEO of JP Morgan, and Mark Zuckerberg, CEO of Meta.Getty ImagesJPMorgan Chase won't allow outside artificial intelligence agents to acces
body: Jamie Dimon, CEO of JP Morgan, and Mark Zuckerberg, CEO of Meta.Getty ImagesJPMorgan Chase won't allow outside artificial intelligence agents to access customer accounts and operate on their behalf, CEO Jamie Dimon said Tuesday, citing risks to the company and its customers as tech firms including Meta release autonomous assistants. "We're not going to allow just any … outside agent to come in inside the company, because it's just too risky for clients and for JPMorgan," Dimon told analysts on the bank's third-quarter earnings call."You don't want rogue agents, and it could be thousands of them," he added, describing the potential threat to customers. In July, an OpenAI model hacked into AI company Hugging Face's servers.  The stance from Dimon, the longtime CEO of the biggest U.S. bank by assets and a de facto spokesman for the U.S. financial sector, is reminiscent of an earlier fight with fintech firms over access to customer data. JPMorgan moved to charge data middlemen including Plaid for access, a dispute that similarly pitted the bank's security concerns against tech firms' demands for access.A JPMorgan spokeswoman confirmed to CNBC that the bank currently blocks external AI agents from operating on behalf of retail customers."Protecting our customers is our top priority. Because it is not safe, we do not permit third parties to access accounts by obtaining customers' banking credentials and logging in on their behalf," the spokeswoman said."We support secure, customer-authorized data sharing through open banking providers and are committed to enabling agentic connections securely," she added.That means that AI agents can access some customer data from Chase accounts in a read-only fashion, such as customer balances, if Plaid or another connector has the user's credentials. But they can't send money or pay a bill — actions that make an agent useful.There's no timeline for when the bank would have safeguards in place to allow agents to directly interact with customer accounts, the spokeswoman added.'Liability transfer'Dimon said JPMorgan is using AI agents internally and plans to deploy them for customer-facing applications. The bank's approach, he said, isn't about being for or against the technology, but about ensuring it serves customers safely.In recent weeks, JPMorgan began a targeted pilot for its own AI tool called Smart Cash, which aims to predict a user's cash flow and move funds to maximize yield, Chief Financial Officer Jeremy Barnum said Tuesday. That would appear to be a defensive move against external agents.Dimon also seemed to draw a line about liability when customers authorize outside AI agents to act on their behalf. "If people are using them, they should understand the risk," Dimon said. "They should understand there's a liability transfer."Personal agents have gained mainstream popularity in recent months as AI models integrate more autonomy, like the ability to cancel subscriptions or use credit cards on a user's behalf, for example.Instinct, a digital concierge that relies primarily on text messaging instead of an app, launched earlier this year on an invitation-only basis. The startup behind the service, San Francisco-based Spear Street Technology, was founded last year and reached a $10 billion valuation last month.  In September, bank stocks were hit as Meta's Muse agent topped the app download charts shortly after it was unveiled, sparking fears that consumers would use agents to move funds from low-yielding accounts to higher-yielding ones. Weeks later, OpenAI released its own agent, Dots. Apollo Chief Economist Torsten Slok and others pointed to the risks that agents pose to cheap bank deposits. But that risk will be limited if agents aren't allowed to operate freely with customers' accounts.

schema.headline: JPMorgan Chase blocks outside AI agents like Muse, Instinct from directly accessing accounts

title: Oil prices rise after IEA warns on market constraints; Saudi officials say Aramco facilities attacked
description: Iran's medium-sized oil tankers continue to wait off the coast of Bandar Abbas at the Strait of Hormuz in Hormozgan Province, Iran on September 09, 20
body: Iran's medium-sized oil tankers continue to wait off the coast of Bandar Abbas at the Strait of Hormuz in Hormozgan Province, Iran on September 09, 2026.Anadolu | Anadolu | Getty ImagesOil prices were higher on Wednesday morning, pulling back from earlier gains, as investors digested the International Energy Agency's latest monthly report on the shape of the oil market. Brent crude futures, the international benchmark, were 20 cents higher at $105.89 a barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate was up $1.27 to $95.41 a barrel. Stock Chart IconStock chart icon Brent The IEA's October Oil Market Report, published Wednesday, warned that constraints on diesel markets could continue well into 2027, with fresh attacks on Saudi Arabia threatening to derail a recovery on the supply side of the global oil market. Fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthis continues to escalate, with the Saudi Ministry of Energy saying Wednesday that an administrative building belonging to oil giant Saudi Aramco had been attacked overnight. No injuries were reported at the site in Dhahran, a city on Saudi Arabia's eastern coast. It follows a series of Houthi attacks on the Saudi capital Riyadh over the past week, including a fatal strike on the city's international airport. According to Al Jazeera, Houthi energy terminals and fuel reserves in Yemen were struck by a Saudi-led coalition, though a spokesperson said that precautions were taken to avoid "collateral damage on civilians." Tensions also continued to simmer between the U.S. and Iran. U.S. Central Command rejected claims by the commander of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy that the Strait of Hormuz is under Iran's control and that any approaching U.S. Navy warships would be "sunk.""RGC's navy commander has no navy," CENTCOM said in an X post, adding that "American forces and regional partners clearly control the Strait of Hormuz." Stock Chart IconStock chart icon Wti Oil may rally another $20-$25 due to the Iran conflict, hedge fund manager and noted commodity trader Paul Tudor Jones said on CNBC's "Squawk Box." "I am long oil... bullish oil...I think it can rally another $20 or $25 bucks," said the founder and chief investment officer of Tudor Investment. "If something to ameliorate the situation was going to happen, it would have happened already before the midterms," he added.

title: Netflix to lay off roughly 1,000 employees, or 6% of workforce
description: The Netflix logo is displayed at a company office on May 12, 2026 in Los Angeles, California.Justin Sullivan | Getty ImagesNetflix said on Wednesday i
body: The Netflix logo is displayed at a company office on May 12, 2026 in Los Angeles, California.Justin Sullivan | Getty ImagesNetflix said on Wednesday it will lay off roughly 6% of its employees, or roughly 1,000 workers, according to a memo obtained by CNBC.The job cuts will largely impact the product, tech, legal and HR teams. "Our mission - to entertain the world - is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritize our people and resources," Netflix co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters wrote in the email to employees. "Our business is strong and growing, and we remain on track to deliver our full year forecast. We'll continue to invest aggressively in high impact areas to improve our service and further drive growth and innovation. "Doing that means making focused choices across the business so we can keep delivering for our members, partners, employees, and investors," the note said. Netflix said it did not have additional comments beyond the co-CEOs' memo. The company is due to report quarterly earnings on Oct. 20. The layoffs come just a few weeks after Sarandos told attendees at the Bloomberg Screentime conference that the company was "not growing as fast as I want."Netflix has faced a paradox in recent months. It continues to post solid profits and remains the biggest player in the streaming realm, but its viewing time has stagnated and the main driver of new subscriber acquisitions has been its password-sharing crackdown and the launch of a cheaper, ad-supported tier.Netflix's biggest threat has been YouTube, but looming on the horizon is Skydance. The combined entity of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery has plans to integrate the two companies' streaming platforms, Paramount+ and HBO Max.Netflix has diversified its content in recent years, expanding into live sports, documentaries and video games in order to compete for share of consumer attention. At the same time, it's lacked the water-cooler-type hits like "Stranger Things" and "Squid Game" that previously boosted subscriber growth and viewership.And Netflix is not the only company looking to cut costs in the media space. Last month, Disney said it would lay off around 300 employees, with the majority of cuts coming from human resources and technology roles.— CNBC's Julia Boorstin and Stephen Desaulniers contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Netflix to lay off roughly 1,000 employees, or 6% of workforce

title: Treasury says largest U.S. banks let politics influence who received banking services
description: A sign is displayed at the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) headquarters at Constitution Center on June 1, 2025 in Washington, DC. Kevi
body: A sign is displayed at the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) headquarters at Constitution Center on June 1, 2025 in Washington, DC. Kevin Carter | Getty ImagesThe Treasury Department's Office of the Comptroller of the Currency found some of the largest banks serving the U.S. allowed political considerations, public pressure and social concerns to influence decisions about who received banking services, according to a sweeping report released Wednesday.The OCC said it reviewed the nine largest national banks under its supervision, examining nearly 100,000 complaints and about 420,000 pages of documents. It found that all nine had used "reputation risk" policies that lacked "clear," "objective" standards and could disadvantage customers because of their political or religious views or lawful business activities. The findings may lend new regulatory weight to a grievance President Donald Trump has pressed since returning to office. Trump has repeatedly accused and sued major banks of discriminating against conservatives and has said he was personally "debanked" after the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol insurrection, claims banks have denied.The report lands a day after the OCC and other Treasury regulators imposed more than $1.2 billion in penalties on Bank of America over separate anti-money-laundering failures. At the same time, the OCC said it is examining whether banks' efforts to comply with anti-money-laundering rules have themselves contributed to debanking. The review covered JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Citibank, Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank, Capital One, PNC Bank, TD Bank and BMO Bank, which together held a majority of assets at OCC-supervised commercial banks when the probe began last year under a Trump executive order.The OCC stopped short of announcing fines or sanctions Wednesday, but said it is considering additional rules aimed at preventing political or religious discrimination.Among the cases it highlighted: JPMorgan subsidiary WePay closed accounts belonging to merchants selling Trump and conservative merchandise. An internal screening list included terms such as "MAGA," "Make America Great" and "America First," even though the OCC found neither WePay nor JPMorgan had formal written standards for deciding when flagged material amounted to prohibited hate or violence.JPMorgan told CNBC its policies prohibit discrimination based on political or religious views and said WePay's process "did not meet our expectations." The bank said it fixed the issue and has since shut down the business.This is breaking news. Please refresh for updates

schema.headline: Treasury says largest U.S. banks let politics influence who received banking services

title: Morgan Stanley tops estimates as equities trading revenue beats expectations by $909 million
description: watch nowMorgan Stanley posted third-quarter results that beat expectations on blockbuster results in its equities trading franchise. Here's what the
body: watch nowMorgan Stanley posted third-quarter results that beat expectations on blockbuster results in its equities trading franchise. Here's what the company reported:Earnings per share: $3.03 vs. $2.91 LSEG estimateRevenue: $20.34 billion vs. $19.95 billion LSEG estimate The company said profit climbed 6.5% to $4.91 billion, or $3.03 a share. Revenue climbed 12% to $20.34 billion.The firm's equities trading division, long a marquee business for Morgan Stanley, posted a 41% increase in revenue to $5.8 billion, exceeding the StreetAccount estimate by about $909 million.Morgan Stanley cited widespread strength across its equities products and regions, but cited Asia as a source of particular strength in the quarter. The gains in that business helped offset disappointments elsewhere.Fixed income trading revenue fell 7% to $2.01 billion, driven by declines in credit and commodities, which is roughly $260 million below expectations. Investment banking revenue edged 2% higher to $2.16 billion, about $110 million below expectations. The bank cited an increase in advisory revenue on more completed mergers, but declines in equity underwriting on lower IPOs and a decline in fixed income underwriting.Still, the results were "good, but not great," as some business metrics showed slower improvement in the quarter, Wells Fargo analyst Mike Mayo said Wednesday in a note. Morgan Stanley shares declined about 3% in midday trading.The economy is subject to two key forces right now: the boost from the AI buildout and the drag from geopolitical strife, Morgan Stanley CEO Ted Pick told CNBC's Leslie Picker on Wednesday.Starting in early September, concerns with overseas conflict, inflation and surging yields slowed activity across Wall Street, Pick noted."The interaction of the AI phenomenon and geopolitics has been the dominant reality the whole year," Pick said. "It's really two very different stories, and I'd like to think that we are going to have the first narrative, the positive narrative, if we can get some control over the geopolitics."Pick is "cautiously optimistic" about markets in the fourth quarter, he added.

schema.headline: Morgan Stanley tops estimates as equities trading revenue beats expectations by $909 million

title: Ukraine warns Starlink limits are disrupting military operations as Russia pounds its energy infrastructure
description: Ukraine has accused Elon Musk's SpaceX of imposing new restrictions on its Starlink satellite internet service without warning, disrupting Ukrainian m
body: Ukraine has accused Elon Musk's SpaceX of imposing new restrictions on its Starlink satellite internet service without warning, disrupting Ukrainian military operations. It comes as Russia intensifies attacks on the country's energy infrastructure despite President Donald Trump's proposed "energy ceasefire."Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on defense technology, said Wednesday that SpaceX has implemented a speed limit on Starlink terminals in motion without notifying Ukrainian defense forces, disrupting some missions. Meanwhile, Russia unleashed an attack on Ukrainian energy infrastructure overnight, leaving at least 600,000 people without power in the Kyiv and Kharkiv regions, raising further questions about the "energy ceasefire" announced by Trump on Sunday."There is significant damage to facilities and equipment – at 26 facilities of our power system and four facilities in the oil and gas sector," Zelenskyy said in a post on X early Wednesday.He highlighted a targeted ballistic missile strike against the energy infrastructure that Zelenskyy said should have been covered by the "energy ceasefire" announced by President Donald Trump on Sunday."The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States," Zelenskyy said.The attack comes after the Ukrainian president on Monday accused Russia of violating Trump's proposal that the adversaries stop attacking each other's energy facilities to help bring down the cost of oil and diesel. Both Russian and Ukrainian authorities initially denied any knowledge of an energy ceasefire agreement. Ukraine has since welcomed such a deal, while Russian authorities said talks are ongoing, without confirming whether they have reached an agreement. Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Monday: "Regarding the status of this agreement, we can refer to Zelensky's reaction. When asked the same question, he said he had not heard of such an agreement, would welcome clarification and was ready for a ceasefire," according to the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Starlink disruptionsZelenskyy also said that for the second time this week, Ukraine received no advance warning about Russian ballistic missile launches. The latest unflagged strike on Kyiv damaged a residential building and killed one person and injured six, Zelenskyy said.Ukraine's Beskrestnov said that the Starlink speed restriction currently applies to the StarShield military service package and is set at 100 mph, or about 160 km/h."It is clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation," Beskrestnov said on Telegram. "SpaceX is likely to have taken such measures at the request of the Trump administration," he added in a separate post.SpaceX and the White House have been contacted for comment. title: BlackRock's Larry Fink warns a data center moratorium could trigger a recession
description: watch nowBlackRock CEO Larry Fink warned that a halt to data center construction could trigger an economic slowdown."If we have a moratorium of some s
body: watch nowBlackRock CEO Larry Fink warned that a halt to data center construction could trigger an economic slowdown."If we have a moratorium of some sort in this country, we will be in a recession," Fink told CNBC Wednesday, after BlackRock reported better-than-expected third-quarter earnings early Wednesday.  BlackRock advanced about 1% in late morning trading. "So much of our economy is based on the buildout of this capex," Fink added, referring to the massive investments made to develop artificial intelligence infrastructure.Fink's warning comes as strong, local opposition to data center construction has emerged as a key issue in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, as communities struggle with rising utility costs, water use, environmental damage and questions over investment transparency.While Fink acknowledged fears about the data center buildout, he also noted "most of it is on misinformation." The stakes are high. Wall Street analysts estimate total AI capital expenditures could climb above $1 trillion in 2027 and total in excess of $5 trillion by 2030. "Data centers are not the problem. They're creating more new jobs than ever before," the BlackRock CEO explained. The scale of investment has created demand for construction workers, physical digital infrastructure, AI compute hardware and energy infrastructure to secure grid power, he said.

schema.headline: BlackRock's Larry Fink warns a data center moratorium could trigger a recession

title: Scott Bessent's growth plans aren't enough to tame surging deficit and debt pile, IMF chief says
description: IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva (L) speaks with US Secretary of Treasury Scott Bessent ahead of a morning work meeting to "revive balanced,
body: IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva (L) speaks with US Secretary of Treasury Scott Bessent ahead of a morning work meeting to "revive balanced, inclusive, and sustainable economic growth for the benefit of all" in the presence of the G7 countries, partner countries, the International Monetary Fund, and the OECD, as part of the G7 summit, in Evian, eastern France, on June 17, 2026.  Ludovic Marin | Afp | Getty ImagesBANGKOK — The head of the International Monetary Fund has urged Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to trim the deficit, warning that his plan to lean on growth to tame U.S. Government debt isn't sufficient."Growth of course helps, but it cannot deliver fast enough the necessary adjustments," Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said at a panel Wednesday at the IMF-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok. "Some [fiscal] measures would be necessary."Georgieva said Bessent recognizes that federal deficits and overall debt have grown "too high," and that measures to improve the budget balance and reduce the debt are necessary. But "the authorities very much rely on strong growth in the United States" to bring them down, she said.Bessent and Trump administration officials have touted resilient economic growth, driven by the artificial-intelligence build-out, reshoring manufacturing and tax cuts for consumers, as crucial tools to improve the U.S. fiscal posture."With 3% growth, we grow our way out of this," Bessent said last month. He has argued sustained growth above 3%, combined with spending restraint, could lower the debt ratio and bend the debt-to-GDP curve. U.S. federal debt has exceeded 100% of gross domestic product, once an unthinkable threshold, with the country's public debt load surpassing $40 trillion and on track to break a record set in the aftermath of World War II. The U.S. government has historically spent more than it collects through taxation, committing to unbalanced spending in the decades since President Bill Clinton briefly managed to balance the budget in the 1990s. But debt-financed spending has sharply accelerated in recent years. Trump cut taxes in his first term and signed the first Covid relief packages in 2020, which Joe Biden followed with a $1.9 trillion stimulus in 2021. watch nowThat federal spending helped stave off a recession but also fueled inflation that still weighs on American households and businesses. Before his appointment, Bessent had said he wanted Trump to cut the deficit to less than 4% of GDP by the end of his term, and said in August that the U.S. budget deficit had likely peaked. The U.S. Treasury market has been battered this year with yields climbing to multidecade highs, as investors bet that surging energy costs and heavy AI spending will keep borrowing costs higher. Benchmark 10-year yields hovered near their highest level since 2002, standing at around 5.2% on Wednesday.  Debt pile growsAlthough the budget figures for the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30 have not yet been released, the deficit is expected to top 6% of GDP, compared with 5.8% in fiscal 2025."With the government running an annual budget deficit of 6 percent of GDP, the debt will rise another $7 billion by the end of today—and each subsequent day," Benn Steil, senior fellow and director of international economics at Council on Foreign Relations, said in a Sept.25 note.  Steil also warned that it could be "reckless" for Washington to declare the debt crunch solved by supporting unsupported projections, pressing for spending and revenue reforms. The IMF, which released its October World Economic Outlook on Tuesday, forecasts U.S. growth of 2.3% in both 2026 and 2027, and projects U.S. gross government debt reaching 142% of GDP by 2031. IMF chief Georgieva has also urged governments to set credible medium-term plans to control deficits instead of relying on stronger growth alone, as global public debt heads toward 100% of GDP before the end of the decade, the highest since World War II. Bessent reportedly missed this week's meetings to attend to "domestic engagements."

schema.headline: Scott Bessent's growth plans aren't enough to tame surging deficit and debt pile, IMF chief says

title: 10-year Treasury yield jumps as September core inflation comes in hotter than expected
description: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange during morning trading on September 16, 2026 in New York City. Michael M. Santiago | Getty Im
body: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange during morning trading on September 16, 2026 in New York City. Michael M. Santiago | Getty ImagesThe 10-year Treasury note yield rose on Wednesday following the latest U.S. inflation print.The yield on the 10-year Treasury note — the main benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — jumped more than 7 basis points to 5.289% and reached the highest level since Oct. 8.The longer-dated 30-year U.S. Treasury yield — which tends to react most to geopolitical events — was up more than 3 basis points to 5.602%. The 2-year Treasury — which closely tracks the Fed's interest rate decisions — gained more than 10 basis points to 4.895%. Earlier, it hit its highest level since Sept. 29.One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely.The consumer price index rose 3.7% year over year in September, higher than the Dow Jones consensus estimate of 3.6%. Core inflation, excluding food and energy prices, came in at 2.6% on an annualized basis, versus the 2.5% consensus estimate. The latest inflation reading comes just two weeks before the Fed's next interest rate decision. With inflation remaining sticky, the central bank may need to raise rates higher and keep them there for longer in 2027, said Christopher Rupkey, chief economist at Fwdbonds."The bond bulls have turned around and are running the other way as 10-year yields have shot higher after today's shocking inflation report," he said. "Inflation is alive and the only way the Warsh Fed knows how to kill it is with another dose of higher rates."Odds for an October 28 quarter-point hike in the fed funds rate — currently 3.75% to 4.00% — increased to 43.7% from just 22.1% a day ago, according to futures trading measured by CME's FedWatch tool.There is now a greater than 95% chance of at least one hike before the year is out, and included in that is a 40% chance that rates are higher by a half-percentage point — double the odds one day ago.Looking ahead to the rest of the week, investors also await the September reading for the producer price index, September retail sales data and weekly initial jobless claims figures, all due on Thursday.— With additional reporting by CNBC's John Melloy.

schema.headline: 10-year Treasury yield jumps as September core inflation comes in hotter than expected

title: ASML says it's getting order interest through 2030 as profit smashes expectations
description: ASML said Wednesday that some of its customers are expressing interest in placing orders for its critical semiconductor tools for 2029 and 2030 as the
body: ASML said Wednesday that some of its customers are expressing interest in placing orders for its critical semiconductor tools for 2029 and 2030 as the company reported third-quarter profit that beat expectations.The comments will likely comfort investors who have been looking to assess the longer-term demand outlook for ASML's lithography machines."Our customers continue to increase their short- and medium-term equipment demand forecasts with us, driven primarily by their views on the size and duration of AI-related investments," CEO Christophe Fouquet said in a press release. "In light of their demand visibility, some customers are expressing an interest in placing orders with us for 2029 and even 2030."ASML is the only company in the world that produces extreme ultraviolet lithography machines, a key tool used by the likes of TSMC to make the world's most advanced semiconductors. Investors closely watch the Dutch company's earnings for signs of AI-related chip demand. watch nowFouquet said current supply planned for 2027 and 2028 will not fully meet the demand of its customers. The company is "investigating ways" to increase capacity for 2028 beyond the 30% increase it had previously forecast. ASML has now updated its guidance three times this year, upping its full-year forecast for the second time in July, and on Wednesday it raised the lower end of its sales forecast for 2026. The company now expects net sales of between 44 billion euros and 45 billion euros ($49.3 billion to $50.4 billion). The previous lower end of the forecast was for 43 billion euros.ASML also said it expects fourth-quarter net sales of between 14.2 billion euros and 15.2 billion euros. The upper end of the range is ahead of LSEG consensus estimates of 14.2 billion euros.  ASML's stock was around 2% higher in early trade in Europe. Shares of the company have rallied 56% this year. Stock Chart IconStock chart iconASML shares year-to-dateDuring the quarter, Samsung and TSMC, the world's two biggest chipmakers, committed to using ASML's High NA extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines. High NA EUV is ASML's next-generation tool, which analysts see as key to the Dutch firm's future growth.For the third quarter, here's how ASML did versus LSEG consensus estimates:Net sales: 11.66 billion euros versus 11.72 billion euros expectedNet profit: 4.96 billion euros versus 4.1 billion euros expected ASML sticks to China forecast The semiconductor equipment maker said it expects China sales to account for 20% of its total business, sticking to a prior forecast.While ASML holds an effective monopoly on EUV machines, a July report from The Information suggested an unnamed Chinese company had begun manufacturing an immersion deep ultraviolet lithography (DUV) machine, citing people familiar with the matter.ASML dominates the manufacturing of DUV machines, which are less advanced than EUV. China has been ramping up its domestic semiconductor supply chain, with some investors concerned it could challenge the European and U.S. dominance. However, analysts raised questions about China's ability to ramp up its own DUV technology. ASML meanwhile has faced challenges in China over the last few years. The company is restricted from selling EUV and some DUV tools to China.

schema.headline: ASML says it's getting order interest through 2030 as profit smashes expectations
